question: Combining the Memory Hierarchy Triangle chart (Figure 5.20, page 229) and the On-Chip SRAM Cache diagram and text (Figure 5.23, page 232), why is SRAM placed at the top apex of Figure 5.20 despite requiring 4 to 6 transistors per bit, and how many 4-byte integer elements (A[0]..A[x]) are fetched from DRAM into SRAM on a single 64-byte cache miss?

tool_calls.query: Figure 5.20 Memory Hierarchy Triangle apex SRAM cache page 229
Figure 5.23 SRAM 4 to 6 transistors 64 bytes 16 elements A[0] to A[15] cache miss page 232

answer: In Figure 5.20 (page 229), SRAM (Technology 1, cache memory) sits at the top apex closest to the processor because it is the fastest storage technology and resides directly on-chip with the CPU (Figure 5.23, page 232), avoiding slow off-chip bus transfers and needing no refresh. Because each SRAM bit requires 4 to 6 transistors (taking much larger chip area than DRAM's 1 capacitor), SRAM is limited to a few KB to a few MB. On page 232, when a cache miss occurs on A[0], the cache fetches a 64-byte line from DRAM; for 4-byte integers, 64 / 4 = 16 consecutive elements (A[0] through A[15]) are brought into SRAM, turning subsequent accesses to A[1]..A[15] into cache hits. [openstax-ics-2024, p.229] [openstax-ics-2024, p.232]

question: According to Section 3.5 (Sorting Algorithms, page 127), how do Insertion Sort and Selection Sort compare in best-case versus worst-case time complexity, and why does Insertion Sort achieve O(N) best-case runtime on an already-sorted list?

tool_calls.query: Insertion sort Selection sort best case O(N) worst case O(N^2) already sorted page 127
Section 3.5 elementary sorting algorithms comparison

answer: On page 127, Selection Sort always requires O(N^2) quadratic time in both the best case and worst case because it repeatedly scans the entire unsorted remainder to find the minimum element. Insertion Sort has an O(N^2) worst-case runtime (on a reverse-sorted list), but achieves an O(N) linear best-case runtime when the input list is already sorted (or nearly sorted) because each new element only needs a single comparison against its immediate left neighbor without shifting elements. [openstax-ics-2024, p.127]

question: According to Section 5.2 (Computer Levels of Abstraction, page 209), what three key characteristics must every algorithm have to be executable and useful on a computer, and why does an algorithm that counts all even numbers fail?

tool_calls.query: unambiguous deterministic finite reasonable amount of time counts even numbers page 209
Section 5.2 key set of characteristics algorithm 100 years

answer: On page 209, every algorithm must have three key characteristics: (1) it must be unambiguous (each step is well-defined and precise), (2) it must be deterministic (reproducible and repeatable so the same inputs always produce the same output), and (3) it must be finite and consume a reasonable amount of time and storage (an algorithm taking 100 years is useless). An algorithm that counts all even numbers fails the finiteness/reasonable-time requirement because there are infinitely many even numbers. [openstax-ics-2024, p.209]
